comments.author: framebolt
comments.text: Semi-OT, but the aside in section 6 about the CI fleet running on donated decade-old laptops derailed my whole afternoon. The only reason those machines are still alive is that they were built repairable: socketed RAM, a battery you swap with one screwdriver, service manuals that assume you will open the case. I have replaced the battery, keyboard, and fan on mine three times over and it still builds a kernel faster than my locked-down work machine dies trying.

replies.author: solderjoint
replies.text: Those machines were repairable mostly by accident. Component integration just wasn't tight enough yet to solder everything down. Modern boards trade sockets for signal integrity and battery life. It's not a conspiracy, it's physics plus margins.

replies.author: framebolt
replies.text: Physics explains the RAM. It does not explain the glued-in battery or the parts catalog that only sells to authorized shops. One is engineering, the other is a business model.

comments.author: hingecrack
comments.text: I bought one of the modular laptops last year, the kind where every part has a QR code and a printed guide. The premium was real, maybe 20 percent over an equivalent sealed machine. But when the battery started swelling at month nine, I had a replacement fitted in ten minutes without shipping anything or arguing about warranty coverage. That one transaction converted me.

replies.author: thermalpaste
replies.text: Same experience with the keyboard. What surprised me is resale value: repairable machines hold it, because the next owner knows a worn battery or a dead fan is a thirty-dollar fix rather than a death sentence.

comments.author: voidcheck
comments.text: The viewpoint that never gets represented here: most buyers will never open the case, ever. They pay the repairability premium and the weight penalty for an option they do not exercise. For the median user, a sealed machine with a solid warranty and cheap out-of-warranty service is strictly better. Repairability is a niche preference this crowd mistakes for a universal good.

replies.author: torxdriver
replies.text: You don't have to open it yourself for it to pay off. The corner repair shop does, and their quote is a third of the manufacturer's because spare parts are actually purchasable. Serviceability benefits plenty of people who never touch a screwdriver.

comments.author: sleekfan
comments.text: Unpopular in this thread, but the industry already tried thick, socketed, and swappable. We called them workstation bricks. The market chose thin, light, and long battery life by an overwhelming margin. Soldered components are how you get a 13-inch machine that weighs a kilogram and runs 18 hours. Repairability is not free; it costs exactly the things most buyers rank first.

replies.author: hingecrack
replies.text: The current modular machines are within a few hundred grams and an hour of battery of the sealed flagships. The gap that once justified soldering everything has mostly closed. What remains is habit and parts-margin protection.

comments.author: torxdriver
comments.text: The interesting development is not consumer choice, it is regulation. Repairability scoring and spare-parts availability rules are starting to force catalogs open regardless of what the market chose. Once vendors must stock spare parts for seven years and publish service manuals, the premium shrinks and this whole debate settles itself by default.
